claims.statement: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that automated systems operate under delegated authority and face structural limitations requiring external ethical oversight.
support.passage: Important decisions that impact human lives, livelihoods, and the natural environment are increasingly being automated. Delegating tasks to so -called automated decision-making systems (ADMS) can improve efficiency and enable new solutions. However, these benefits are coupled with ethical challenges.

actions.findings: Automated decision-making systems introduce significant ethical and operational challenges when delegating high-stakes tasks without external auditing. [source-43c0a60d013d4369]
actions.limitations: The available literature examines ethics-based auditing and cognitive offloading rather than direct empirical demonstrations of autonomous methodological self-correction.
actions.next_questions: What formal architectures would enable an automated system to reliably surface and test its own foundational premises?
actions.reason: Synthesizing available source material on automated decision-making and cognitive extension to address the project question.
actions.summary: Analysis of automated decision-making and cognitive systems indicates that while algorithmic frameworks can process complex tasks, identifying and revising foundational methodological assumptions typically requires external oversight and normative evaluation.
actions.title: Limitations of Automated Epistemic Self-Correction
